div.head: SCENE I.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: What a horrible dull place this old castle is! Not a soul worth looking at, and nobody to speak to either, but the old earl and father Ambrose. I'm sure, if I were my young lady, I'd no more stay to be pent up with such a set of frights—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Heigho!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Heigho?—That's a melancholy note, ma'am; worse than the cuckoo's in a rainy June. The very sound of it puts me in the vapours.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I'm very uncomfortable.—Heigho!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Nay, you must not go on in this way; you'll make yourself ill in good earnest. You have no idea how it alters you. I'll be hang'd if my lord does not begin to suspect—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Good heavens! What do you mean?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I'll tell you, ma'am. I happen'd to meet him yesterday in the long gallery. “Can you tell me,” said he, “what makes my daughter look so shockingly?”—He said so indeed, ma'am.—Then, ma'am, he went on. “I suspect,” said he, “that all is not right here.” And with that he thump'd his breast and star'd me full in the face. “I'm sorry,” said I, “that your lordship has any thing the matter with you there; you'd better,” said I, “take some advice; father Ambrose,” said I—“Father fiddlestick,” cried he: “I mean my daughter, hussy!” said he—“Poor dear lady,” said I, “she can do you no good.”—“But I can do her some good,” said he; “a husband,” said he—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: How you alarm me—Surely either you or father Ambrose must have dropt some hints—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I, ma'am!—If ever I dropt a syllable either about Sir Albert, or Maurice, or your secret marriage, or my own—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Hush, my dear girl! don't talk so loud.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: For me to blab indeed! Or for father Ambrose—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I believe you; but every thing alarms me. Alas! What have I not suffer'd, during the three tedious years since my Albert was torn from me! Never once to have heard from him, not even to know whether he yet be living—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I'm sure, ma'am, I've a fellow feeling with you; for, if you have lost Sir Albert, I have lost my poor Maurice, and a kind-hearted soul he was, and a good husband too, though he was no gentleman. But why do I say so?— For he was promoted to be Sir Albert's esquire in the Holy Land, and that's a gentleman's post. But come, ma'am, keep up your spirits.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: That is beyond my power. Even hope itself seems to have abandon'd me.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Heaven forbid! It's the best friend we have.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Aye, girl, but like many other friends, it is apt to desert us when we most require its aid.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Well, after all, 'twould be some comfort to know whether our husbands are likely to come back to us.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Fie, Matilda, what a way of talking!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Lord! ma'am, how hastily you take one up. I was thinking what Sir Reginald would say—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Sir Reginald! What's he to me?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Not so much, poor man, as I fancy you are to him. He does so look at you, and sigh—and he's a handsome man, ma'am, and a generous one too let me tell you.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: What is all this to me?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Nay, ma'am, I don't know; but in my mind, if he were not so serious, he would be a very pretty fellow.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: If you go on in this way, I shall begin to suspect you—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Me, ma'am! I wish I may never have worse luck. No, no! he flies at higher game.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: How you rattle! Sir Reginald is a gallant gentleman and my father's friend; but as for thinking of me, thank heaven! that is out of the question. But hark! Some one's coming I am sure.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Dear ma'am! Nothing but a rat in the old wainscot.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Nay, I am sure there is some one. As I live, my father and Sir Reginald. Don't you see them in the gallery?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Sure enough they are there. If my lord is not giving him the history of old Sir Topaz and his picture! Don't be alarm'd, ma'am, they can't have heard a word. There, sit down and take your work—I'll sing you the ditty of Poor Ellen, and that will look natural, you know.

div.stage: Enter the Earl of Clare and Sir Reginald.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Heyday! here's a catterwauling!—I didn't know thou hadst this talent.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Oh my lord! I have many perfections which your lordship has not been able to find out yet.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Certainly I have not made the discovery. Well, Ethy, so you did not expect us—we stole a march upon you.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I did not expect your lordship so soon.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Why you seem sad, love.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Matilda was singing a pathetic ballad, sir, of an unfortunate maiden, whose father tore her from her lover. It happen'd long ago.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Aye, I dare say. I've heard of such fathers. An old niggardly hunks, I warrant me. Fathers now-a-days are different sort of creatures. Come—don't look so grave. I'm not such a miserable, tyrannical puppy; I love my dear girl too well to treat her in that way. I can feel for you—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Oh! your lordship's tender feelings are well known.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Not better than your assurance, Mrs. Pert! My tender feelings indeed!—Lookye, Ethy, so far from depriving thee of a lover, child, I wish to give thee one.— Come, come, never look so shy; I know it all—all about that little heart—You thought I couldn't find it out.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Lack-a-day, my lord, you distress my lady so—it's not fair to joke about serious matters.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: No, Ethy, I'm quite serious, I assure you; never more so in the whole course of my life. I have a husband for you, my girl—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I hope your lordship will go through with your good work, and give me my hushand too.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: So! the disorder runs in the family, does it? Aye, aye, you may take him if you please, and I wish him joy of his bargain. But now, Ethy, to our business. What would you say now, if I were to throw you at once into a husband's arms?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: How—where—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Just by, love—close at hand—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Oh dear sir! keep me not in suspense—say—say when, how came he?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Half an hour ago—on horseback—
— Now's your time—now or never—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: But, my lord, you see my lady's impatience. It's quite cruel of you to keep her in suspense.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Egad! that's true—so it is indeed.—Well, Ethy, my dear, to make you happy at once, here he is!—
Now for a look and a speech—kneel, you happy dog!

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: How shall I find words, madam—but heavens! you tremble, madam, you—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Stand out of the way—What's the matter, madam?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Nothing in the world but over joy. Leave her to me.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Lean upon me, ma'am.—Pray, my lord, don't speak to her.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Matilda, is it you?—My head feels quite confus'd—I hardly know where I am—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: In the drawing-room, dear, at the end of the gallery.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Oh my dear father! if you have any compassion—if you love me—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Love thee, Ethy! Why thou know'st I do, and so will Sir Reginald too.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: How can you go on so, my lord? Don't you see my lady is getting worse again?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Well, child—best go into the fresh air—sudden joy sometimes takes this turn. Go with her, Matilda—But hark thee—now we understand one another, the sooner the business is finish'd the better. We'll have the wedding to-morrow morning.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Name not to-morrow!

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: No! why not? Is not to-morrow as good as any other day? You little simpleton! making such a fuss about nothing—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Do let me speak to you, sir—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: No sort of occasion—we understand you perfectly— there—get you gone—I'll take care of every thing— leave it all to me—
Toll loll de roll!
Well, Reginald, you see I've done your business.

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: I wish, my lord, I could discover such cause for triumph.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Why you've no more penetration—she could not conceal it. Not perceive her affection was fix'd?

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: Not on me, I fear.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Not on you, sir? On whom else should it be fix'd?

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: That is more than I know. But her visible confusion—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Pshaw! What a novice in love must you be, not to discover the trick of all that? She forgot herself a little for a moment, I must confess; though, when the first burst was over, she brought herself off in a great stile. Let the women alone for that, egad! There's not one of 'em—Her mother, poor dear woman! did just the same, when her father announc'd me as her future husband.

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: But, my lord, if my conjecture should prove true—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Don't plague me with your Iffs, don't put me out of temper, when I never was so well pleas'd in my life; but go—do your duty—enquire after her health—do what you please—but get out of my way, for I must hold a council of war with my subaltern officers about the feast to-morrow. Egad! I'll make old Clare Castle ring again.—
—Geoffry! Arthur!—What a cold blooded fellow that is now—Geoffry, I say!—Where are all the knaves?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Did your lordship's honour call?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Yes, my lordship's honour did call; and where were you, ye idle knaves, that you didn't come when I call'd?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: I'll tell your lordship's honour all about it. We were sitting in the buttery, my lord, Arthur and I, just comfortable like as it were, drinking your worshipful honour's health in a horn of ale; for, said I to Arthur—

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: No, that's not it neither—I'll tell your lordship how it was. Says I to Geoffry, Geoffry, says I—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY
sp.p: Have you no more manners than to stand prating thus? Can't you learn of me? When do I put in my oar?—
It was all as I told your noble lordship; for, says I to Arthur—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: With all my soul. Do hold your tongue, and attend to me. I am about to marry my daughter to Sir Reginald de Clifford, and have fix'd on to-morrow morning for the wedding—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Arthur, give me thy hand, my brave boy!

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Take it, i'faith! This is rare news. We shall have noble sport.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: We'll make the cellar bleed. Rare humming ale—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Aye, aye, all in good time, and plenty of it too. But now for my orders. In the first place, let all care and anxiety be banish'd from the castle and its neighbourhood. When my own heart is light, no other shall be heavy if I can help it. So let a general holiday be proclaim'd.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Ah bless your worship's honour! Let Geoffry alone for that.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Let all comers have free welcome.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: I warrant me. That's my look out as porter.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: And d'you hear, Geoffry. You must away to the town, and order in a fresh supply. Let there be plenty of every thing.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: I'll be off directly.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Hark ye, Arthur, we'll have the minstrels.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: There's not one within twenty miles of the castle who shall be absent. I know their haunts—Giles Grinder, Simon Squeak, and the rest of them.—Odds my life! we'll foot it merrily.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Well, set about it. Away, away!

div.head: SCENE II.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Every thing seems to be in a state of confusion. I can't make out what is going forward. I met Sir Reginald e'en now. “Give you the good day, Sir Knight,” cried I. “Good day!” quoth he, “that's as it may prove,” and off he bounc'd like an arrow from a cross bow. I met Geoffry our butler, bustling along with a face full of care. “Master Geoffry,” quoth I, “what's the news?”—“News enough,” quoth he, “beef, mutton, hog's puddings”—and poph! off he bounc'd too.—So, here comes Arthur. Peradventure he may be more reasonable.
Well met, honest Arthur; thou art merry this morning. I would have a little talk with thee.—Why what is the matter with thee?—Stand still, thou naughty knave, and tell me what hath happen'd.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Marry, that I will. Great news, my master, rare news, i'faith!—Have you heard it?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Heard what?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Why the news.—I could have sworn now that his reverence Father Ambrose, chaplain and almoner of this here castle—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: But the news—

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Aye, marry, the news—Now what does your reverence think the news is?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: That would I learn from thee.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Why the news is—
—Od's my life! that's a knock of authority.—The news is—
—Nay, if thou art in a hurry I am not —As I was saying, the news is—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Fie, Arthur, linger not thus, but open the gate.—
—Nay, now it passes—

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: So doth not he who knocks. But to pleasure thee, father, I will perform my function.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: How now, thou untaught peasant! Am I, Sir Hildebrand, to wait thy ignoble leisure?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: What's that? Untaught peasant? Ignoble leisure? Who are you?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I have the honour to be the representative of the most illustrious lord the Baron Von Poppindorff.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: What, little Poppindorff, the Jew broker, who bought young Scatterall's ruin'd castle at t'other end of the forest?—I'll tell thee what, Hildebrand—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: What means the boor?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Boor in thy teeth, if thou com'st to that—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Nay, I pray thee, Arthur, restrain thyself. Be pleas'd, sir, to acquaint me with thy purpose.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I come to announce the Baron's immediate approach. His lordship would confer with the Earl of Clare.—
—As I live he is arriv'd, and no preparation, no one in the way to receive his lordship, not a soul, as I hope to be sav'd.—
—Wilt thou stir? Wilt thou announce his lordship's approach?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Not I. Announce it thyself, Hildebrand. This is my station.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I will report thy contumacy to my lord the baron.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: A fig for the baron!

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Give over, I pray. I will myself give the proper directions.

div.stage: Enter Baron Von Poppindorff and three Servants.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What is all dish? Nopoty in the way? Where is Sir Hildeprant?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND
sp.p: Here, my good lord.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Here, my goot lort!—For why you think I keep a you for, that there is not nopoty to receive a me?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: My very good lord, blame not me. The fault was not mine. But this ill-manner'd porter—

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Nay, the fault was all his own.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Believe him not, most gracious lord. He is a foul-mouth'd varlet. Nay, he revil'd your noble lordship with his filthy phrases. “A fig for the baron,” said he—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: A fig for the baron! And pray what was you do, when he say a fig for the baron?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I—I—my lord, I was about to chastize him.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: 'Tis well for thee thou wert only about it. By this staff of office—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: What is towards now? Arthur, what means this?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Nay, an I know.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Put down thy staff, and keep the peace.—My lord, the Earl is at present occupied, and may not be interrupted; but, 'till he shall be at leisure, I request your lordship to enter and repose yourself.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I am varra mush ill-treated, sir—a baron of Yarmany!

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I pray you, my lord, be appeas'd.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: No, sir, I will not be appeas'd. I will teach a you all—A baron of Yarmany indeed!

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: Enter Sir Albert and Maurice, as Pilgrims.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Stay, good Sir Albert—have a little compassion on your faithful servant, who has follow'd you so long over these rough cross roads, that the sight of a shady grove, where he may rest his weary limbs, and hold a little private consultation with the contents of his knapsack, is a temptation there is no resisting.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Courage, good Maurice.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Why, as for courage, neither I nor any of my generation ever wanted their proper share of it. But the foes we have to deal with now give themselves mighty little concern, about either big looks or hard blows. Hunger and weariness are enemies, which in the long run will come off victorious. For my part, I'll dispute the matter no longer with them.—Here's as pretty a bank to repose upon—

div.stage: (Sits down and takes out a bottle.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: For shame! Relax now, when we are almost arriv'd at our journey's end? Don't you see Clare Castle just before you, and don't you know what treasures it contains?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Perfectly; and I know too what treasures this contains. Won't you taste it, sir?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Not if it were nectar! I have no appetite, no sense for any thing, but for the joys which my fond imagination pictures. Ah! if you felt like me the mix'd sensations of transport and anxiety, which fill my bosom when I review those well known walls after an absence of three years—

sp.speaker: MAURICE
sp.p: Three years! On my word, 'tis a long interval, during which a number of curious things may have occurr'd. Not that I would insinuate aught against the lady Ethelinde—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Breathe not a sound which may impeach her faith!

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Heaven defend me from such profanation!—And yet, when I think of three years—But hold—Who comes here?—I should know the—As I live, sir, old Geoffry, the drunken butler from the castle. Let's stop him, sir, and make some enquiries before we proceed.—Odso! you have forgot your whiskers—So—now you are pretty well transmogrified.—He seems in a mighty hurry—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Plague on it! this service is fatiguing; and then there's such a number of things to remember.—

—Let me see—aye—the butcher—hum— the baker—aye—grocer, gamekeeper, cook—Egad! he's at work already, with his whole army of scullions, pellmell, slashing away, spits, pans, pots—But I must get on. 'Twill be noon presently—Heyday! whom have we here? Pilgrims?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Kind sir, we are bound to our lady of Walsingham, to return thanks for our safe arrival from the Holy Land. But we are strangers, sir, and have lost our way in the forest. Pray what castle may that be?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: What, not know Clare Castle! You must be strangers indeed. But you are come in good time—There's rare work going on there now—plenty of good eating and drinking. You shall have your share. All comers are welcome.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: May we presume to ask, kind sir, what has occasion'd all this festivity?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: You may. None can tell you so well as I. Do you know me?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Alas! sir, we are strangers.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Not know me! That's good i'faith!—Well to see now—Not know old Geoffry, the butler of Clare Castle, and now appointed steward of the feast, that's to be held in honour of the lady Ethelinde's wedding!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Confusion! Ethelinde's wedding!

sp.speaker: MAURICE
sp.p: Be patient—
—the lady who, sir, was you pleas'd to say?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: The Lady Ethelinde, only daughter and sole heiress of the Earl of Clare. To-morrow's her wedding day, i'faith! There's monstrous preparation making—all the country invited—fat oxen kill'd—sheep, pigs, lambs, ducks, capons, pullets—minstrels, morice dancers, mummers, strummers—nobody idle—all at work—men and boys—woman and maids—But I'm in a vast hurry— I must away to the town, to buy stores and all manner of provisions—sugar, salt, spices, pepper, ginger, nutmeg, cinnamon and cloves, oranges and lemons, quince marmalade and currant jelly. I've not a moment to lose —I must be back again incontinently—nothing can go on without me. By your leave, gentlemen—you'll be heartily welcome at the castle.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: One moment, sir. To whom is the Lady Ethelinde to be married?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Oh! I'll tell you. To Sir Reginald de Clifford. He lives just by—a mighty convenient distance—a mere step —But I must be gone, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: And have they long been attach'd?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Why, as to the matter of that—it's not a bad story— poor dear lady!—My lord, they say, suspected some time ago that she had a secret kindness for the knight— likely enough too, for, to say the truth, he's a portly gentleman—so what d'you think he does?—Egad, sir! when she least expected it, he popp'd the question upon her, and out it all came.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: All what?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Why all about her love. A full confession, i'faith! And so my lord, bless his heart for a good worthy nobleman as he is!—sends this morning for Sir Reginald, and makes him a fair offer of her hand. A great match, you know—fine girl—vast fortune—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Avow her love! Prodigious!

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Yes, mighty prodigious—never any thing known like it—pining and moaning, whimp'ring and whining—but they say she's merry enough now—nothing like a young husband—But, out upon it! what am I doing here?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: With your permission, sir—Is there no other young lady at the castle, sir? No pretty young lady?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Why how should you guess that now? I warrant me you mean madam Matilda.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Is that the young lady's name?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: It's a pretty one, isn't it?—Ah! the lord help you! she's a good one.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: How, sir?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Why, now, if you were but to know her—though she's a good girl enough too, if you can get fairly about her. But then you must let her have her own way, or else she's the very devil incarnate.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: I suppose, sir, you are well acquainted with her.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: You may say that—leave me alone for the girls—Know her, quotha! There's never a crook nor a turn about her, that I don't know as well as my way to the cellar.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: I suppose, sir, she's in no want of admirers and sweethearts.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Sweethearts! That you may say—Ah bless your heart! I could if I'd a mind—but hush! It's not fair to blab— though I could tell you something—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: So she's not hard hearted?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Ah ha! You want to get it out of me, do you?— Hard hearted! That's as it may happen.—There's one, I believe, she likes—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Some smart, lively fellow, hey? Such, for instance, as a gentleman of your appearance and qualifications.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: I? He! he! he! you comical toad you! You have guess'd it, have you?—Why, to say the truth, she does come to a little, her ice does melt—a cup of canary sometimes, when I catch her alone in the buttery—a little bussing and touzling and squeaking—I could tell you such secrets—she's a dear loving soul, that's the truth on't—But I must he gone—The goodness of the day be with you, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Here's a discovery!—Well, sir, you perceive what three years have brought about.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Away, Maurice! let us instantly to the castle. She shall not carry it in this triumphant way.—Oh false, inconstant Ethelinde! Oh sad reverse of my long cherish'd hope!

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: A pretty sort of conduct to be sure—What! with such a wither'd old sinner as that!—Odd's my life! I could have forgiven her if she had shewn a better taste!

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: Enter the Earl of Clare and a Servant.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Who is it you say wants to speak with me?

sp.speaker: SERVANT.
sp.p: One as calls himself Baron Poppindorff. He lives hard by.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Shew him in.
I have heard of this Poppindorff. A Jew broker, who calls himself a baron. What can the fellow want with me?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Mine varra goot lort, the Baron Von Poppindorff has the honour to pay his respect to your goot lortship.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: I am the baron's humble servant. Pray what are your commands with me?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I have no command, my goot lort; but, as I have made little porchase in the forest, I have thought it my duty to make a my compliment to your goot lortship.— You have varra fine place here, on my wort—fine house, fine forniture, fine every thing—it must have cost mosh varra great deal of monesh.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: I suppose so.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: You suppose so? What! you not know what it cost? You keep a no account how you spend your monesh? That be varra foolish.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Mighty civil of you to say so. You are very regular in your own accounts, I presume.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: To be sure. I keep a big book, where they all are put down so prettily—all the items and the sum totalsh. Ah! it would do your heart goot to see how grant they look.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: So, you have made some money, have you?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Pick'd up some little traifle, some small matter of two three hundred thousand marks. Ah these wars, these crusades to the Holy Lant! On my wort, that Saladin has been the best friend I have. The Christians go fight with him for Cherusalem, and the Chews they pocket their monesh. I often make my little joke, and say, Your varra humble servant, Mister Saladin, you make a me varra rich mans.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: You seem to have a strong sense of the obligation; but I don't perceive how I have any concern in it.

sp.speaker: BARON
sp.p: Ah! my goot lort, I ask your pardons. I will tell a you with your goot leave. I have just porchase one house, castle what you call, t'other side of the forest, where I mean to live and enjoy myself and my little monesh. I have try; but I find it so lonesome to be always by myself, the day pass so slow, so tedious, and the nights so disagreeable.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: You don't find your solitary reflections very amusing then? You discover that something besides money is wanting?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I beg pardons—Monesh is varra goot, varra pleasant to look at, to count over; but then one want some variety. So I have think it might be better to have some society, somebody to talk to when the weather is bad.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Your plan then, I presume, is to marry.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: The varra thing, my goot lort, I was go to say. To get a pretty little wife, so kint, so goot humour—I was think, my goot lort, that as you have one dochter, who they tell a me is varra pretty womans—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: The deuce they did!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: We might make a the match.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: I'm prodigiously oblig'd to you—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I knew you'd say so. They was tell a me you was a varra sensible old gentlemans.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: And so you shall find me, I can tell you.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I make no doubt. I am varra glad I have made acquaintance with you. I like your looks.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: I wish I could return the compliment.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: You are in goot luck I can tell a you. I will settle handsomely on my wife; and no doubt you will settle this castle and all your estates and monesh—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Aye, to be sure—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I was think so—upon me and the heirs of my body. Ah! how glad you will be to see one, two, three pretty little childers running about and calling you grantpapa. The little Isaacs, and the little Solomons—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: The little imps of the devil!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Imps of the teifel! What way is that of talking of your own grantchilders? Oh fie, fie! I thought you had more sense than to talk so of your pretty little grantchilders.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: My grand children!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: To be sure—must not your own dochter's childers be your grantchilders?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: And so you have the modesty to propose yourself, in good earnest, as a husband for my daughter?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Yaw, mynheer.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: My daughter is dispos'd of.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What you say dispos'd of?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Aye, and will be married to-morrow to Sir Reginald de Clifford.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Has he the monesh?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Enough to answer my purpose.—Good morrow.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Stay, stay—What for you go away and leave a me all alone?—Scorn a me and my monesh! Scorn a the Baron Von Poppindorff!—I will be revenge—I will teach a you—Where is Sir Hildeprant? Where are mine squires?

div.head: SCENE V.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Stand aside—What are you all crowding here for?— You, sir, get out of the way—
Hey! whom have we here? Who are you?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Save you, good sir. May two wayfaring pilgrims, newly return'd from the Holy Land, partake of the hospitality of this noble castle? We would not be troublesome, sir.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Then you would be other than you are, sir. We have trouble enough already I think, without the like of you, so you may be off—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Clear the way there for the steward of the feast!— Heyday! What's toward now?—Arthur and my two worthy pilgrims?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Stand aside, master Geoffry—let me discharge the castle of these vagabonds.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Not so, good Arthur. These pilgrims are other than thou tak'st them for. They are my friends. I met them in the forest e'en now, and bad them to the feast.—How are ye, my hearty fellows?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: An it be so, they may stay and welcome.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: So, you are all here—William, my boy—Cicely, my girl—Kate—Peter—Humphrey—Welcome all.—But, bless my heart! we are losing time—There's the deuce and all to do—brewing, baking, roasting, boiling— sweeping the rooms—brushing away cobwebs—Off my boys—get along, wenches—the buttery's open—rare humming stuff—Be sure you drink the bride's health.—
—You're heartily welcome, my noble pilgrims! Come along, Arthur!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: All is confirm'd then! She is false and I am miserable.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: False enough! But bear up, sir. You see I am not so overcome—But what's that?—Two women, if my eyes don't deceive me—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: 'Tis the perfidious fair herself—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: And Matilda with her, by all that's changeable!—If the villain be not laughing!—I'll make you laugh to some purpose before we part, I will!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: How lovely she looks! Can falsehood reside with such perfection?—I'll speak to her, Maurice—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: You are too much agitated at present. Try to recover yourself a little. Step aside for a moment.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Say no more, Matilda! My embarrassment is beyond all bearing. Surely there never was any thing so cruel and perplexing as my situation!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I protest, madam, for my part, I don't see any thing so very distressing in this business. I know a good many young ladies, who would settle it very easily.—Bless me, ma'am, look there—
—Pilgrims, I declare, and by their crosses and escalops must come from the Holy Land. Perhaps they may be able to give us some intelligence. Speak to them, ma'am.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Pray, sir, as you seem to have come from the Holy Land, may I venture to ask—did you know—that is, did you ever chance to meet—a young cavalier—a handsome young gentleman—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Madam!

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I ask your pardon, sir, but I wish—I have a particular —a very particular reason, which I cannot just now explain, for wishing to know whether you ever was acquainted—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: With whom, madam?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: The young gentleman, sir, I spoke of.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: You spoke of no one, madam.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Dear ma'am, how sadly you set about this business! Let me cross examine him a little. I'll engage for't I'll make him speak.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: That's as you may give him opportunity, madam. Now, if I guess right, you'll find so much to say yourself—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Indeed, Mr. Sauce-box! Why then I'll begin with you. Come now, tell me—Do you come from the Holy Land?—Did you know one Sir Albert de Mortimer there? Can you tell me if he is alive or dead? Can you—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Which of your questions, madam, do you choose I should answer first? Or would you prefer my answering them all together?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Don't be provoking now, but tell me.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Why yes, ma'am, I do confess as far as relates to the Holy Land—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Well—and Sir Albert—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: And as for Sir Albert, madam—there might be such a person—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Might be?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: That is, madam, there was. By the same token, he had a very agreeable, accomplish'd young man with him as his esquire, one Maurice, madam.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Did you know him? Do, dear pilgrim, tell me every thing about him. Is he alive or dead? What's become of him? Where is he?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: That's more, I fancy, than he knows himself. Do you know him, ma'am?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Psha! no—that is, yes, a little—and what of that?— Well—and so—this Maurice—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Have you any particular reason—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: To be sure I have. But what's that to you? Do tell me what you know about Sir Albert and Maurice.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: If you know them, madam, perhaps you may be able to direct us to one Father Ambrose. We have a commission—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: From whom?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: And about what?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: That's a secret. For, said he, take heed, said he—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Who said so?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Sir Albert, madam; and said Maurice—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Was that a secret too?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Inviolable—for, said he, take heed, or Matilda—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: What! Did he speak of me?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Of you, madam? Then, perhaps, that lady is the lady Ethelinde?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: How should you know any thing about her?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Lord, madam! the whole country rings of her ladyship. —Pray, madam, is it true that her ladyship is to be married to-morrow?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Aye, madam, is it true?—And yet you talk'd of an nterest—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I did so indeed. I have a very strong interest, sir. To say the truth, some events have occurr'd—matters have recently taken so unexpected a turn, that—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Then, madam, I am to conclude that the report of your intended marriage is true—

div.stage: Enter the Earl of Clare and Reginald.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Ha! Ethy! Overtaken you at last—what! chatting here with these pilgrims? Fine likely fellows—
—Well, you are come in good time— you'll meet with plenty of every thing.—Sir Reginald, why don't you do your duty? Let your bride stay for you!

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: I am here, my lord, obedient to her commands. The highest honour I can enjoy is to receive them.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Well said. Eh, Ethy! not a word in reply?—Never mind—you'll get rid of that shyness by and by, I warrant me. But come along—if we stand talking here we shall be too late—the mass is just beginning, and the father prior will take it mightily amiss if we interrupt him at his devotions.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: By heaven! this is not to be borne. What! in my presence to go off hand in hand with him!—Let us hence, Maurice, never to behold her more.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: One moment's delay, if you please; for here comes a personage, who, probably, may have it in his power to give us some useful directions.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I am lost in astonishment. She marry! I know not how to believe it—and yet there's no getting over the evidence.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Reverend sir—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I am not at leisure.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I beseech you, reverend sir, if it be but for a moment. We would communicate with one Father Ambrose.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: That is my name. What would'st thou? I know thee not.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: No one in these parts does know me, sir. If, sir, you are Father Ambrose, I would ask whether you know Sir Albert de Mortimer.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: What of him? he was my dear and valued friend. Know'st thou aught of him?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I knew him well, sir. We were together in Palestine. He charg'd me to impart to you—But are we private, sir?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Fear not; no one will interrupt us. Well—proceed.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: He wish'd me, sir, to pray you would vigilantly watch over his interests—that the Lady Ethelinde—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Alas! deceiv'd, unhappy man!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: How, sir?—Deceiv'd?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Aye, deceiv'd. Her marriage with another is announc'd, and to-morrow—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: To-morrow! No. Thank heaven! I am come in time—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Thou!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Yes, my honest, faithful friend!—Behold in me that wretched Albert—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: And Maurice too, sir, at your service.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I rejoice to see thee. It is well thou art come. I was almost at my wit's end.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I fear I am come but too soon. To see every hope blighted, every fancied joy annihilated—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Why truly the case is somewhat novel and embarrassing.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: 'Tis horror—distraction!

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: And it requireth calm consideration.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Talk of calmness to a man, whom disgrace and misery threaten to o'erwhelm! Is she not to be married tomorrow?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: That's true indeed. What can be done? Not a step can be taken, without disclosing your secret marriage, and then, heaven bless us! we shall have a pretty piece of work.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Please your reverence, of two evils that will be the least. And yet I know not—We certainly are two very unfortunate personages. I have pick'd up a curious account of my rib too.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Of madam Matilda?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Of madam Matilda. She's agog too.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I protest I know not. It may be so. Madam Matilda, to be sure, is of a lively temperament, of a sanguine constitution, which ordinarily is indicative of amorous propensities.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Od'slife! I could almost have pass'd it over, if she had given me a better substitute—but such a miserable whipper-snapper—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: No more—Tell me, good Ambrose—What would you advise?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: It is a weighty matter, and, as I said, requires mature consideration. I will reflect upon it.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: You talk as if there were time for deliberation, when every moment calls for decision.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Nay, nay, there is time enough. We have the evening before us. Stay—aye, that will be best—Rememb'rest thou my chamber? There—on that side of the gateway—Come thither after sunset, when we will discuss the matter further. By that time, the festivity in the castle will be at its height, and thou may'st enter unobserv'd.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: But where can I pass the tedious interval, before I may venture to your chamber?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Let me consider—Thou canst not have forgotten the hermitage in the forest. Thither repair 'till sunset. Yet hold—on further reflection, let Maurice remain here, that, should any thing material occur, he may advertize thee.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: For a time then farewell! My fate and happiness are in your hands.

div.head: SCENE I.
div.stage: The Forest. A Hermitage in the distance.
Enter Baron Von Poppindorff, Sir Hildebrand, and Servants.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Hold a your foolish tongue, Sir Hildeprant, and your bibble babble about patience. I tell a you I will be revenge. —To be refus'd for a knight, a poor paltry—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Mushroom!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What a you say?—A presumptuous, contemptible—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Braggadocio!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What teifil's breeding is that to interrupt me at every wort? What you mean to make echo of me?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I humbly beg your lordship's pardon; but, when I found you profess'd yourself to be in a passion, I thought it my duty to be in a passion too.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: To be sure.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: A pretty pass indeed the world is come to, for my lord the baron to be treated at this rate!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Aye, aye, 'tis varra goot—But never mind—I will be revenge, Sir Hildeprant—I will do soch thing as shall make a him repent his insolence. What you think I shall do?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: If I were your lordship—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Let a me alone—I have the thought. I will—I will— What would you do now, if you was in my place?— Something varra terrible, varra dreadful—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: By Saint Anthony! I'd carry off his daughter—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Goot!

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Marry her—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Goot! goot! The varra thing I was think of myself. We'll do it to-night!—But stop—There is the servants—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: No danger there. The cellars were all open before we left the castle, and they'll have had their dose before night, I warrant them.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Then I fear them nicht. We'll do their business.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: The only question seems to be, who is to do it?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Who? Why you, and mine other peoples.—What for you shake a your head?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Marry, my lord, it would not be amiss if there were more of us. Make the most of us, we are but five.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: But five?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: We may easily enough be counted; and, for some of them, if your lordship could infuse into them a small portion of your own valour, it would not be the worse for them.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I was no think of that.—What can be done?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Suppose, my lord, we were to beat up for recruits? A few stout fellows would remove the difficulty.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: The varra thing I was just think of myself. But where can they be found?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Now the wars in Palestine are over, there are plenty of vagrant soldiers—sturdy pilgrims—hardy knaves who have smelt blood—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Hardy knaves who have smelt bloot!—Goot—But where can they be found?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Why here's a fellow approaching—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Where?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: There—Don't you see him among the trees? A kind of pilgrim looking fellow. Shall I try to engage him?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Yaw.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: He will probably expect something by way of earnest. I must trouble your lordship to unloosen the strings of your purse, and furnish me with a small matter. As I am a true man, I have not a single sous.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Unloose my porse! Give my monesh! What you think I do with my monesh, to give it away?—Tell a him the Baron Von Poppindorff be varra generous, and will reward a him. Give my monesh indeed! A pretty joke!

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: May Pharaoh and all his ten plagues go with thee, thou mean-spirited stingy curmudgeon! To have seen better days, and to be reduc'd to serve this rascally Jew money-changer!—Had I but a good name, whereby to get into another service, I'd starve with him no longer. But my necessities compel my abasement. Now for the scurvy commission wherewithal I am charg'd. By the mass! the pilgrim is a likely knave—
I give thee the good day, pilgrim.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: The good day to you, sir.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: May I inquire what brings thee hither?

sp.speaker: ALBERT
sp.p: A good familiar question—
—I purpose, sir, to visit yon hermitage. Have you any further commands?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: In faith, thou art a pretty looking fellow, and not like one that dealeth in hermitages. Tut! man, I know thee.

sp.speaker: ALBERT
sp.p: The deuce you do—
—You have the advantage of me, sir, in that respect, for I never saw you before in my life—
—and I hope I never shall see you again.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: You may be glad you have seen me now. I have taken a liking to you—thou hast a martial demeanour, as though thou hadst seen service—Ah! there's a kind of expression, as it were of valour, which cannot escape a soldier's eye.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Are you a soldier, sir?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Canst thou behold me, and ask!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Why really, sir—but, however, since you are pleas'd to say it, it may be so.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Come now—confess—Am I not right?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Yes, sir, I have serv'd.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I could have sworn it. I rejoice to hear it. I love a soldier at my heart. And after all thou art poor! 'Tis pity! What if I were to put thee in a way to redress the wrongs of fortune?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: You are somewhat rapid in your advances, sir—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I will prefer thee to the service of a noble, a generous friend of mine. Thou must undoubtedly have heard of his excellency the Baron Von Poppindorff—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Never in the whole course of my life.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: A nobleman of acknowledg'd courtesy, valour, and liberality.—Shall I intrust thee with a secret?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I have no curiosity to know what does not concern me.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Thou shalt find that thou hast a concern. My noble friend, who dwelleth close at hand, hath a controversy with a neighbouring lord.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: May I inquire who his adversary is?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: They call him Clare.

sp.speaker: ALBERT
sp.p: This may be worth hearing—
Clare?—Pray, sir, what may be your friend's cause of quarrel?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Why, sir, this Clare—d'you mark me—hath refus'd to give my illustrious friend his daughter—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: To give her as what?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Marry, sir, as his bride. Now, sir, my noble friend, unable to stomach so gross an affront, hath meditated a revenge commensurate with the provocation.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Of what nature?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Thou shalt be instructed. He is purpos'd this night to assail the Earl's castle, and bear away his daughter. If thou wilt engage in the enterprize under my guidance, my noble friend, the epitome of honour and generosity, will reward thee beyond thy hopes.

sp.speaker: ALBERT
sp.p: What an infernal project!

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Is it not a glorious plan?—Come, my brave fellow— what dost thou ruminate upon?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I was considering—Is it quite certain that the Baron means to carry his project into execution to-night?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Positively so.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Well, sir, I have reflected on your offer, and think I may as well make one of your party.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: There spoke all the nine worthies at once!—What! I knew thou hadst it in thee—come—I will introduce thee to the Baron.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: All in good time, sir; but I pray you, excuse me for some half hour or so. I will but perform my vow at the hermitage, and will follow you.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Be it so.—That is the road to the Baron's castle. When thou arrivest there, ask for Sir Hildebrand.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Farewell, noble Sir Hildebrand! If such be the man, what must be the master?—What ought I to do? Repair to Clare Castle, and give notice of what is going on?—No—I will first visit the Baron, and ascertain more distinctly this abominable conspiracy against the peace and honour of my Ethelinde.—My Ethelinde!— she is no longer mine!—But lost to me as she is, though her falsehood has for ever blasted my happiness, I cannot, I will not abandon her.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: How unlucky it was, ma'am, that my lord came upon us, and interrupted us in our conversation with those pilgrims! I dare say, we should have been able to have pick'd up some intelligence.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: It was indeed provoking. They said, you know, they had been charg'd with a commission from my Albert to Father Ambrose—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: To be sure they did.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I wish I knew what it was. Do you think you could find out the pilgrims, and discover what it was they were charg'd with?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I'll go directly, ma'am, and try.—But see—if Father Ambrose himself be not coming this way—I dare say he knows it by this time. Leave him to me, ma'am—I know how to come round him.—I'll get it out of him, I warrant.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: You seem to have a pretty good opinion of your abilities.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Lord! ma'am, were you but to see how I manage him —I've a sort of taking way with me, which these old gentlemen can't withstand—
Oh my dear sir! I'm glad you're come—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Stand aside, I pray thee—my business is with thy lady.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Nay come—you shan't be cross now—do smile and be good humour'd—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Art thou in thy right wits?—Away!—I have no time for trifling.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Why you old, cross, ugly thing—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Stand aside, I tell thee again. Trouble me not.—
What is the meaning of this, daughter? I thought to have seen thee in tip-top spirits, all alert and merry; but thou seemest melancholy.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Alas! father, can I be otherwise, when my heart is weigh'd down with sorrow?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: What! when the whole castle and the country for ten miles round are running mad with joy, because thou art to be married to-morrow? Oh daughter, daughter! could I have expected this from thee?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Reproach me not, good father: though I may well reproach my own weakness—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: There now—with what ingenuity can some people gloss over their own faults!—Weakness, call you it? Give it its proper name—Don't mince the matter.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I will not cavil with you about words. Call it whatever you please; but indeed I am not guilty of what you suppose. My faith and constancy are unimpeach'd—Never for a moment have I been false to my Albert.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Not false to thine Albert? How cam'st thou then to accept of Sir Reginald?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Accept him! Sooner would I quit this paternal roof, and encounter the rude buffetings of an unfeeling world, than falsify my vow to the husband of my heart.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Wherefore then suffer these preparations to go on?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I have tried to prevail on my father—but my apprehensions of a premature discovery—and you know his way—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Oh ho! now I begin to understand.—Well, I am glad to find matters are not so bad as I expected. Come, be of good cheer; I have receiv'd some intelligence.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: What! you have seen the two pilgrims then? Do now tell us what they say, that's a good creature.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: It was a secret.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: How can you be so provoking!—When my lady is so curious, and I should be so glad to know—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Must thou be always prying into every thing? I would have thee conquer that evil propensity.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I'm sure you're always snubbing one—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I would not offend you, father, by appearing too inquisitive; but, if there is nothing improper in my asking—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Nothing in the world can be more natural. The communication, as I told thee, was, and for the present must remain, a secret. But this much I may venture to say— Sir Albert lives.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Heav'n's blessing on the news!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: And Maurice—Do tell me what they said of him.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: For this once I will satisfy thee. He lives too.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Oh you dear delightful man!

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: But, father, if I may believe your looks, you could tell me something more. Consider how anxious I must be—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Well, perhaps, I may be able—these pilgrims—by the way, they are very gentleman-like pilgrims. I have taken a great fancy to them.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I don't care about the pilgrims—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: No!—That's strange.—Well, well, they give me good hopes that Sir Albert is on his return, and will shortly be here.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Let me then fly to my father, explain every thing, and put an immediate stop to these odious preparations!

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Softly, daughter—add not to thy former error the new one of precipitation. I must again consult the pilgrims, ere I can decide on what is to be done. I have given thee enough for pleasant contemplation, and for the government of thy conduct.—The blessing of the evening be with thee!

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Well, Matilda—my Albert will return—my sorrows are over, my cares are forgotten.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Oh lord! ma'am, I never was so delighted in my life— I shall love a priest as long as I live for the sake of this old gentleman, though he was so crusty.—How glad our poor husbands will be to see us!—When do you think, ma'am, they'll come?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I wish I could tell you.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Well, ma'am, never mind; we shall have them soon for certain.—No more melancholy now, no more sighing and groaning!—For my part, I could sing and dance— Couldn't you, ma'am?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Yes, my girl—I feel as light as air. Hope once again illumes my heart, and visions of happiness open to my view!

div.head: SCENE III.
div.stage: The Gate of Baron Von Poppindorff's Castle.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: If my direction had not been so plain, I should begin to suspect I had mistaken my way.—But soft—what is this?—A baron's residence?—It seems marvellously out of repair.—All fast too—Let's see whether it contains any inhabitants.

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: Who's there?—Stand!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Pray, sir, is this the residence of the Baron Von Poppindorff?

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: And if it be, what then?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: In that case, I would inquire for one Sir Hildebrand.

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: Sir Hildebrand? What dost want with him?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I would speak with him, sir. 'Tis at his bidding I come.

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: Why then belike thou art the soldier pilgrim he said would come here?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: The very same. Pray advertize him of my arrival.

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: That be more nor I dare do. I munna leave my post. Our baron, plague take him! be a main out of the way cantankerous sort of a chap. But I'll call him, sir.— Our castle be not so large, but he'll hear me fast enough.—Sir Hildebrand! Why, Sir Hildebrand, I say!

div.stage: Enter Sir Hildebrand within the gate.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Wherefore all this clamour, master Simkin? Hath any thing untoward happen'd on thy guard?

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: I know not what thou call'st untoward. I've seen nothing of that sort. But yonder's a man—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: What, my man of war!—Open the gate forthwith, Simkin, and let him enter.—Nay hasten—Thou art always so tardy—

sp.speaker: SIMKIN.
sp.p: I be doing it as fast as I can—Don't hurry a body so— A plague on this old lock!—There—I've don't.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND
sp.p: Welcome, my bold fellow! I have spoken of thee to my lord the baron. Enter.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: After you, sir.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: I perceive thou hast learned courtesy in the service. Follow me then, my man of war!

div.head: SCENE IV.
div.stage: An Apartment in the Baron's Castle.
Enter Sir Hildebrand and Sir Albert.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: This way.—Repose thyself in this chamber for a moment, while I announce thee to my noble friend. There are, thou seest, accommodations—Thou may'st amuse thyself with surveying the portraits, wherewithal the apartment is decorated. They're his noble lordship's ancestors, all undoubted originals, and strong likenesses.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: His lordship's ancestors!—They certainly must be originals, for they are like nothing that ever was seen before.—But who comes here?—The baron himself, I presume.—He has a mighty Israelitish appearance.

div.stage: Enter the Baron and Sir Hildebrand.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: This, my good lord, is the person of whom I spoke to you. You see he is a fine likely fellow.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Yaw, varra fine, varra likely indeed—Hark a you, Sir Hildeprant—

sp.speaker: ALBERT
sp.p: Why this is the very fellow, who was drumm'd out of our camp at Messina for usury. I remember him perfectly.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: So, friend—What is your name?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I understood, sir, it was my sword, and not my name you wanted.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Goot, varra goot; 'tis your swort indeed. Sir Hildeprant was tell a me you have been in the wars. Had you moch fight?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I had a few opportunities of seeing service.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Ah! there was hart work, I dare say. But never mind—Sir Hildeprant was say, he tell a you what we are about.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: He mention'd something of a plan to carry off the Earl of Clare's daughter.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Yaw! I will carry her off, and make her my wife.— Well, friend, what you say? Have you the goot heart?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: You may depend on it, wherever you go I'll not be far behind you.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Thank you, friend, varra moch oblige; but I shall expect you to go before a me, I can tell a you.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Excellent well, my lord. The conceit is good.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Yaw—I think it be varra goot for him to go first, when I pay him the monesh. What you think I pay him the monesh for, but to go first?—
—'Tis your trade, you know. Come, tell a me—When was it you went to the wars?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I join'd our army at Messina—'twas on the fourth of May—I shall never forget the day—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: For why you no forget?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! It was such an excellent thing! 'Twas enough to make one die of laughing!

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What was the joke? I love the joke. I sometimes make a the little joke myself. Come, tell a me your joke.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: You'll like it vastly. I got to Messina, just as they were drumming a rascally Jew money broker out of the camp.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: The teiful you did? And pray for what you call that a joke? It was varra bad joke.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! They laid it on him heartily, and the rascal look'd so dismally, and made such a howling! 'Twas rare sport—Ha! ha! ha!—He must have felt them, you know, pretty smartly.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: No doubt.—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Why you don't laugh—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I ask your pardons, I do laugh great deal—Ha! ha!—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I knew you'd like to hear it, 'tis so droll. He was a precious fellow. They all said flogging was too little for such a blood-sucking rogue. He ought to have been hang'd, they said.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: They were varra uncivil persons for their pains. But bless a my heart! Sir Hildeprant—run away, and send in my arms and my weapons, The pilgrim shall choose for himself.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I need them not. Mine own are deposited in the forest; and I have moreover a companion, upon whom I can depend, and whom I doubt not I shall be able to engage for this enterprize, if your lordship should wish to have him.

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Engage him, my lord, by all means.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: For why you interfere? The varra thing I was just think of myself.—
—Yaw—engage him by all means.—Where is he?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: I agreed to meet him about sunset at the hermitage.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Go—run away—bring him here directly—
So—now we shall be goot troop, and need not fear noboty. —Ah ha! mine jackanapes lort! I will teach a you how to scorn me and my monesh!

div.head: SCENE V.
div.stage: Geoffry, Arthur, Maurice, and others, discovered sitting at a Table, with Bottles and Glasses.

sp.speaker: OMNES.
sp.p: Hurrah! Here's to my lord again!

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Well said, my noble hearts! You're all kindly welcome, and there's plenty for you. So fill again to the health of our young lady.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Were the horn a mile deep, I'd see to the bottom of it. —Here's to her good fortune!

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Not forgetting Madam Matilda. Ah! she's a girl of the right sort.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: That she is, I'll be sworn; and so you know, master Geoffry, as well as any one.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: I?—What should I know?

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Ah you sly rogue! We understand you.—Dost not think we know thee of old?—That buttery of thine, could it but speak, I warrant me could tell us a comical secret or two—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Fie, Arthur—gentlemen never talk of such matters —When a pretty girl—It's not fair to blab, you know.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: No more it's not, master Geoffry.—Well, here goes to madam Matilda. Why how now, pilgrim! Not fill thy glass?—What makes thee so dull, man, o'th'sudden?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: I dull?—Not I—I protest I never was so merry in my life—Ha! ha! ha! What you say is so droll!—Here goes to madam Matilda—Come, master Geoffry, confess —Tell us a little more how you and madam Matilda go on.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Not I—I'm too much a man of honour for that. If a fine girl, you know, takes a fancy to one, mum's the word—Why now what brings that Father Ambrose here, to interrupt us just at the height of our mirth?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: So, my good friends! All got together merry and happy? I'm glad on't. I like to see cheerful faces.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: That's more than some of your cloth do, with your penances and fast-days. But mayhap you look forward to confession time. You'll bring us up then.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: When that time comes, master Geoffry, it will be soon enough to talk about it. I'm not in my function now; so go on with your merriment, and give me a glass of your liquor.—That's well—Fill it up—Here's to your young lady's health!

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Well swigg'd, i'faith!—I didn't know thou had'st this in thee.—Come, my lads, his reverence sets us a good example.—Fill up your glasses, and do him reason.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE
sp.p: Hist! A word—I have convers'd with the lady Ethelinde —all's right in that quarter—she is faithful—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: And Matilda—

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Nay, I know nought of her—But hark!—Sir Albert is here—he hath made discovery of a plot—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Of what nature?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Hush! We cannot discourse of it here.—He requireth thy assistance, and that forthwith. Let us slip away, and I will tell thee more.—Now's the time—Follow me.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Are you all ready, my lads? Here we go to his reverence—How now! His reverence off?—And, as I live, carried off the pilgrim too!—If ever I was play'd such a trick since I first tasted liquor—

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: Never trust me, if they ben't gone to find out the girls. Let your friars and pilgrims alone for that.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: We'll be after 'em directly—We'll only empty the can. Good old sack must not be slighted. And to add a zest to the liquor, suppose, Arthur, thou giv'st us a song.

sp.speaker: ARTHUR.
sp.p: For good fellowship's sake, and to pleasure thee, master Geoffry, I will.—Now, charge your glasses, and mind you all strike in with me in the chorus.

div.head: SCENE VI.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Well, ma'am, here we are again, just in the old way. Night's come on, and we don't seem a bit nearer the end of our business. I can't imagine what father Ambrose can mean by his humming and hawing.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I have such entire reliance upon him, that as far as the delay affects only myself, I feel no great uneasiness; though I confess I am sorry that my father is still allowed to persist in an error—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Lord! ma'am, if that's all, there's no great harm in it. He's always taking some strange fancy or other in his head—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Fie, fie, Matilda—He is always affectionate, and his intentions are ever kind. I have reproach'd myself too often for having contracted engagements without his participation, to suffer myself to insinuate any thing against him—But hush!—
—Didn't you hear a noise at the door?—There again—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: As sure as can be somebody's at the door. They're trying to break it open—Oh dear ma'am! if I don't tremble from head to foot—Ah!—

div.stage: Enter the Baron and Sir Hildebrand.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Tell a me which is she—

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: That's your prize—I'll secure the other—Now let's off as fast as we can.

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Ah ha! pretty rogue, you come along with me.—For why you make stroggle—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: If you are men—Oh help! help!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Help! Murder! Fire!

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Plague on your screaming! Come along quietly.

div.stage: Enter Sir Albert and Maurice, armed, with vizors closed.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Hands off, villains! Release this lady—lay hold of that fellow—secure him—Here, give me a cord.—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What teifel's work is this?—Tie a mine hants?—What you mean by tie a mine hants?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Be not alarm'd, lady. You are safe. No one shall harm you.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Whoever you are, sir, receive our thanks. Without your timely succour, what would have become of us?

sp.speaker: BARON
sp.p: So, you tied too, Sir Hildeprant?

sp.speaker: HILDEBRAND.
sp.p: Aye, fast enough. I suppose the ropes will be shifted to our necks soon. A plague on your project!—If you were to be hang'd alone, I shouldn't care—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: What you say, hang't?—Oh dear, oh dear a me!—
—Pray let a me go—I will give you the monesh —moch, great deal monesh.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Oh ma'am! if there are not more people coming along the gallery—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Fear nothing, ladies—We will protect you.

div.stage: Enter Lord Clare, Sir Reginald, Ambrose, Geoffry, and Servants.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Here they are, i'faith!—Have at you, villains!

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Oh my dear father!

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Fear nothing, love!—Down with them, Reginald!

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Stay—the villains are secur'd. These gentlemen, heaven reward them for it! rescued us.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Which are the rogues then?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Here they stand, my lord.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Let me see them. Bring them forward, Geoffry.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Come forward, d'ye hear, and shew your ugly faces— Now the lord preserve us, whom have we here?

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: What! the noble Baron Von Poppindorff!—I'm your most humble servant—And my worthy Sir Hildebrand too!—I am really at a loss to shew my proper sense of your kind intentions Pray what have you to say for yourselves?

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I have nothing to say at all, but that I wish I was not never come here. It was all Sir Hildeprant his fault— he persuade a me, when I no think nothing. Hang a him if you please, but let a me go. That hanging is one thing I never could bear, it is so disagreeable.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: No, no, sir, you sha'n't get off so easily. We'll teach you how to invade Clare Castle.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: If your honour's worship will leave them to us, we'll cool their courage for them. There's the finest cold bath below in the castle moat, a little muddy indeed, and in this warm weather not quite the sweetest. A few plunges there, and a little exercise afterwards in a blanket—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: Plunges and planket!—What you say?—Duck a baron of Yarmany!

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: If I were to treat you as you deserve, I should leave you to Geoffry's discipline. But take them away—confine them with the other prisoners, 'till we can find leisure to-morrow morning to determine what is to be done with them.—Geoffry, see them properly secur'd.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Get on, ye vagabonds!—Troop—march—

sp.speaker: BARON.
sp.p: I do, goot master Geoffry—Oh dear, oh dear a me! I was never get into no such scrape in all my life before!

div.stage: [Exeunt the Baron, Sir Hildebrand, Geoffry and Servants.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Now we've got rid of them, we may think of other matters. By the by, Ethy, who are these gentlemen to whom we are so much oblig'd?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: They are entire strangers to me; but I owe them obligations which I never can repay.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: That's true—very great obligations indeed. Gentlemen, I return you my best thanks. Egad! you came just in the nick of time—Hey!—How's that?—What business, by the by, could you have here at all?—Eh, Reginald?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: That, my lord, Father Ambrose can explain.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: Yes, my lord. Having receiv'd notice of the baron's intentions from two of his associates—these two worthy gentlemen whom you see here—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: The deuce they were!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Not exactly associates, my lord; merely appriz'd of his plan, and solicited to co-operate in it.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: So, so—not associates—only accessaries before the fact.—And have you the assurance—

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: Pray, my lord, suffer the gentleman to proceed. I dare say he will give a good account of himself.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: I can assist him, if it should be necessary.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: You seem to know more of them than they do of themselves; but, if you can, do clear up the matter.

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: That gentleman, having reveal'd to me the baron's plan, departed with his companion to meet the conspirators, not to assist, but to frustrate their wicked project.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: So, so, that was the case!—I'faith! ye are noble gentlemen, and I am thankful to you for your opportune services.—By the way, though, I could do it more to the purpose, if I knew whom I was addressing.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: If my services, my lord, have been so fortunate as to merit your approbation—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Sir, they merit more. I long to know you, that I may prove to you my gratitude.

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: Then, my lord, I thus disclose myself.

div.stage: (He raises the vizor of his helmet.

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE
sp.p: My Albert! My lov'd, my long lamented lord!

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: My lov'd, my constant Ethelinde!

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Heyday! What's all this?—My lov'd lord! My lov'd, my constant Ethelinde!—Be so good, sir, as to stand a little farther off.—Is the girl gone mad?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: If I am, 'tis with joy.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Come away, I say.—What are you doing there, Sir Reginald, to let another man run away with your bride?

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: The truth of our situation has been too long conceal'd from your lordship; but it is now time that all mystery should end. Sanction'd by my royal master, under whose banners I fought in Palestine, I assert a husband's right to this lady.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Husband! Why what the deuce—Eh, Reginald!

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: Your lordship will recollect the fear I express'd of our having been too hasty—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: But who could have guess'd—
—So, you was married all the time, was you?—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Let me implore your forgiveness—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Forgiveness indeed! To make your father a fool—To bring him into a scrape with—Egad! Sir Reginald, I hardly know what to say to you—This little demure— You have been dev'lishly ill-treated in this business.

sp.speaker: REGINALD.
sp.p: Say no more, my lord. Now the discovery, which as you know I always dreaded, is made, I cannot suffer my own personal feelings to damp the joy which it must occasion to others. Let me be an advocate with you in that lady's favour—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: An advocate in her favour?—That's very handsomely said of you to be sure!—
—Well, and what have you to say for yourself, madam?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: I depend entirely on your kindness and good nature.

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: You do?—Why then to shew you what a judgment your's is, I've a great mind—I could find in my heart— not to be angry with you at all.—There—
I forgive you.—Why don't you introduce me to this gentleman?

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Sir Albert de Mortimer, sir—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Sir Albert de Mortimer! the hero who sav'd our gallant monarch's life!—Sir, I am honour'd by your alliance—

sp.speaker: ALBERT.
sp.p: The nobleness of your conduct, my lord—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Say no more about it. Give me your hand, and take her's from mine.—Well Ethy! hey! and how did you manage to carry on this matter so secretly?

sp.speaker: AMBROSE.
sp.p: There I must come in as a party in your lordship's forgiveness. Overcome by their entreaties, I join'd their hands, and, at the same time, united madam Matilda here to Maurice, Sir Albert's esquire.

sp.speaker: MATILDA
sp.p: Y—es, my lord, I co—confess I was married too; but I hadn't my dear lady's luck, my hu—hu—husband isn't come back.

sp.speaker: MAURICE
sp.p: With your lordship's leave—
Yes, mistress, your hu—hu—husband is come back, and a little sooner, perhaps, than you expected.

div.stage: (He raises the vizor of his helmet.

sp.speaker: MATILDA
sp.p: Oh my dear, dear Maurice!

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Hands off—keep your distance—I have heard of your pranks—You know your way to the buttery—Old Geoffry is a pretty sort of playfellow—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: I! Old Geoffry indeed! Is the man out of his senses?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Aye, madam, I know all about it—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Ha! ha! ha! We've done their business. The whole gang of 'em are as prettily pack'd together—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: So, sir, do you dare to say any thing about me?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Aye, sir; that you ever had her alone in the buttery?

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: That I ever suffer'd any improper familiarities?

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: That you ever treated her with a cup of canary? That there was any bussing, and touzling and squeaking?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Sir—madam—I vow and protest—Never was so amaz'd in the whole course of my life—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Speak out, sirrah!

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Don't mince the matter, friend—the lady wishes you to confess the truth. You was more communicative this morning in the forest.

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: So!—You was the pilgrim then?—I'm fairly caught, egad!

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Come, sir, don't stand staring, and humming and hawing, but speak out. What did you ever see in me—

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Nothing, as I hope to be sav'd. A cup of canary now and then indeed—I confess the canary—

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Well, sirrah!

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Nay, don't browbeat my witness. I'll stand by you, friend, you shall have fair play.—So you confess the canary? —Well—go on.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: Aye, go on. The bussing and touzling, sirrah!

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Lord help your heart! Why now I'll be sworn—Bussing and touzling quotha? That were a pretty joke indeed.

sp.speaker: MATILDA.
sp.p: You won't speak out, won't you? Why you poor, dry, wither'd, sapless twig! You little red-nos'd, pimply fac'd—

sp.speaker: ETHELINDE.
sp.p: Come, Maurice, let me settle this misunderstanding. Your Matilda has been my constant companion. I can answer for her attachment and fidelity as I can for my own.

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: There is no disputing your ladyship's testimony.—
—Well, Sir, what have you to say for yourself?

sp.speaker: GEOFFRY.
sp.p: Why, to be sure, the matter is a little awkward. It would seem that, somehow or other, I've got on the wrong side o'the post. But there's no harm done. You may believe what they tell you; and if ever you catch me at bouncing again, without knowing better whom I have to deal with, send me to keep company with the baron.

sp.speaker: MAURICE
sp.p: Well, I am persuaded—What do you stand twisting your fingers there for?

sp.speaker: MATILDA
sp.p: That my conduct should be call'd in question in this outrageous manner, when I'm sure my lady knows, and every body knows—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Psha! I tell you I am satisfied.

sp.speaker: MATILDA
sp.p: It's very hard, I'm sure, that I should be accus'd, and with such an atomy too—

sp.speaker: MAURICE.
sp.p: Be appeas'd, I say. Come—come to my arms, thou spotless dove!—

sp.speaker: CLARE.
sp.p: Why so, that's right. Now, as I take it, all goes as it should. Come, my girl, take your husband's hand. May you be as happy, as the man of your choice can make you! And as for the rest of you, and all our worthy friends, the oftner I see you with smiling faces at Clare Castle the better!
